principles: Fix the root cause (concurrent main-mutation corruption), not the symptom (one specific reconcile path).
Make safety mechanical, not by-convention: a future gap must turn a test red rather than rely on a reviewer noticing.
Lock-only changes: never alter command semantics while adding the lock.
Stay bounded: address the demonstrated risk; defer the maximalist architecture change rather than smuggling it in.
drivers: B-7365 proved a real, long-lived unlocked main-mutating path existed and was missed by convention alone.
The shared-main-worktree fleet model means any other unlocked main-mutating path is a latent equivalent corruption.
There is currently no mechanical guard ensuring every main-mutating path is locked.

options.name: A: lock-coverage + regression guard
pros: Bounded and shippable now; directly closes the corruption-race root.
Adds a regression guard so future B-7365-class gaps are caught mechanically.
Lock-only — low blast radius, no semantic change.
cons: Keeps the shared mutable main worktree; relies on the lock being acquired (the guard mitigates the remaining risk that a path forgets).
Guard must correctly distinguish main-mutating from story-worktree-only paths or it will false-positive/negative.

options.name: B: full per-session checkout isolation
pros: Full per-session physical checkout isolation removes the shared mutable state entirely — no lock needed.
Eliminates the entire class of concurrent-main-mutation races.
cons: Large architecture change requiring its own design decision (truth source: session-ownership-and-write-leases.md).
Out of scope here; would block the bounded corruption fix behind a big rewrite.

rationale: Option A closes the actual demonstrated risk (concurrent main-mutation corruption) with a bounded, lock-only change plus a mechanical regression guard that generalizes the B-7365 fix and prevents recurrence. Option B (full per-session checkout isolation) is the maximalist alternative; it is recorded as deferred and intentionally out of scope, because it requires a separate architecture decision and would delay shipping the corruption fix.

preMortem.scenario: The regression guard mis-classifies a story-worktree-only merge (merging main INTO a story branch) as a main-mutating path and demands a lock it doesn't need.
preMortem.trigger: Static scan keys on the substring 'merge main' without distinguishing the cwd/direction of the merge.
preMortem.consequence: False-positive guard failure blocks unrelated work and erodes trust in the guard.
preMortem.mitigation: Classify by whether the operation writes the main ref / commits on the main checkout, not by substring; cover a story-worktree-only path as an explicit negative (must NOT require the lock) case in the guard test.

preMortem.scenario: A main-mutating path is wrapped in the NON-reentrant withMainWriteLock while already running inside a locked context (e.g. DONE).
preMortem.trigger: CHK-002 wraps a nested critical section with the wrong helper.
preMortem.consequence: Self-deadlock or a thrown 'lock already held' error breaks DONE.
preMortem.mitigation: Use withReentrantMainWriteLock for any path reachable from an already-locked flow; the main-write-lock-smoke reentrancy cases plus a real validate run catch a deadlock.

preMortem.scenario: The guard only checks the paths known today and silently passes when a brand-new main-mutating helper is added later.
preMortem.trigger: Guard hard-codes an allowlist of file:function pairs instead of scanning for the mutation primitive.
preMortem.consequence: The next B-7365-class gap ships unguarded — the exact failure this story exists to prevent.
preMortem.mitigation: Scan for the git-mutation primitives (commit on main / merge into main / update main ref) repo-wide and assert each enclosing path acquires the lock; a newly-added unlocked primitive then fails the guard by construction. Add a negative fixture that introduces an unlocked primitive and asserts the guard goes red.
